newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia has no plans to threaten western interests.
newsitem.headline: Russia has no plans to threaten western interests.

text.p: Russia does not at the moment intend to apply economic sanctions against western countries if NATO goes ahead with its plans to take in some of Moscow's former Warsaw Pact allies, a senior official said.

"The issue of the introduction of economic sanctions towards a series of western countries if NATO expands to the East is not on the government's agenda at present," Itar-Tass news agency quoted first deputy prime minister Aleksei Bolshakov as saying.

Bolshakov was responding to an interview published by Britain's Daily Telegraph newspaper which quoted security chief Alexander Lebed as saying Moscow would hit back at German and U.S. industrial interests if the West allowed NATO expansion.

Lebed's office denied the report, saying Lebed never gave the interview and would not have said such things. It was an attempt to raise tensions between Russian and NATO states, it added in a statement.

The Daily Telegraph quoted Lebed as saying Moscow felt deeply threatened by the Alliance's plans to allow former Communist Bloc states to become members and suggested Germany was trying to build a new empire in the East.
"We follow the strategy closely and will react accordingly. I am telling you that I will therefore have to reconsider the proper attitude to the United States and Germany," he was quoted as saying.
"Let there be no mistake. German and American industrial interests in Russia will suffer directly as a result of enlargement plans."
Lebed said he would explain his opposition to expansion plans when he visited NATO headquarters early next month.

President Boris Yeltsin appointed Lebed as his security adviser three months ago and the gruff former paratroop general, who has made no secret of his own presidential ambitions, has been in trouble before with controversial off-the-cuff remarks.
Russia's policy-making Security Council, of which Lebed is secretary, said the remarks in the article by Carey Schofield had been made up.
"General Lebed gave no interview to this madam. And the quotations which appear in the article have nothing to do with anything A.I. Lebed said to journalists," its statement said.
"(It is) an attempt to sharply increase tension between Russia and the NATO countries, to provoke an outflow of foreign capital; to provoke an upsurge in mistrust towards Russia."
But The Daily Telegraph editor Charles Moore said in a statement: "We are surprised by the reaction of General Lebed's office. The interview did take place as reported. We stand by our story."
Officials from Moscow and NATO met last week in Vienna to hammer out a compromise over the Alliance's plans to accept former Warsaw Pact states as members but the two sides remain far apart.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Tuesday Moscow remained opposed to the eastward expansion of NATO's military infrastructure.

"We do not accept either the idea of the expansion of the NATO military infrastructure to the area of the former and now extinct Warsaw Treaty or the efforts to transform this alliance into an axis of a new European system," he said in a speech to the U.N. General Assembly.

Primakov made clear last week that the stationing of NATO troops and weapons closer to Russia's borders was unacceptable. Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are front-runners to join NATO, probably next year.
